items.followUp: Define enzymes and describe four factors that affect their activity.

rubric.why: Gives the defining role of an enzyme.
rubric.description: Defines enzymes as biological catalysts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an enzyme as a biological catalyst.

rubric.why: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering the activation energy.
rubric.description: States that enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Enzymes act on particular substrates or reactions.
rubric.description: States that enzymes are specific in their action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the specificity characteristic.

rubric.why: Enzymes are not used up in the reactions they catalyse.
rubric.description: States that enzymes remain unchanged or are not consumed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Enzymes work best under particular conditions.
rubric.description: States that enzymes have an optimum temperature or pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either optimum condition.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions.
They lower the activation energy needed for reactions.
Each enzyme is specific to particular substrates or reactions.
Enzymes remain unchanged and are not consumed during reactions.
Each enzyme works best at an optimum temperature and pH.

items.followUp: Describe the main stages of the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies where the Calvin cycle occurs and its relationship to light.
rubric.description: States that the Calvin cycle is a light-independent process occurring in the chloroplast stroma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the location or light-independent nature.

rubric.why: Describes the fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP.
rubric.description: Explains that carbon dioxide combines with RuBP during carbon fixation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the reactants or the fixation step.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions support reduction to carbohydrate intermediates.
rubric.description: States that ATP and NADPH are used to reduce the cycle intermediate to G3P.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this reduction step.

rubric.why: Shows the products and/or continuation of the cycle.
rubric.description: States that some G3P is used to form sugar and the rest regenerates RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sugar formation or RuBP regeneration.

modelAnswer: The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis and occurs in the stroma of chloroplasts.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP and is fixed into a three-carbon compound.
ATP and NADPH are used to reduce this compound to G3P.
Some G3P is used to make sugars, while the rest regenerates RuBP so the cycle can continue.

items.followUp: Explain how humidity, wind, light and temperature affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Higher temperature generally increases evaporation from leaf surfaces.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher temperature generally increases the rate.

rubric.why: Humidity affects the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of humidity on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that high humidity reduces, or low humidity increases, the rate.

rubric.why: Moving air removes moist air from around the leaf.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of wind or air movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking air movement with increased transpiration.

rubric.why: Light commonly causes stomata to open, while darkness tends to close them.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light on transpiration through stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking light or darkness to stomatal opening or closing and the rate.

modelAnswer: Higher temperature increases evaporation of water from leaf surfaces and generally increases transpiration.
High humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient from the leaf to the air, so transpiration decreases; low humidity has the opposite effect.
Wind removes moist air around the leaf and increases transpiration.
Light usually causes stomata to open and increases transpiration; in darkness, stomata tend to close and the rate decreases.

rubric.why: Biogeography concerns where organisms occur across geographical areas.
rubric.description: Defines biogeography as the study of the geographical distribution of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the study of distribution and 1 mark for referring to organisms and geographical regions.

modelAnswer: Biogeography is the study of the geographical distribution of organisms in different regions of the world.

items.followUp: Differentiate between an ecosystem and a community.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of the same species in an area.
rubric.description: Defines a population as individuals of the same species living in the same area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the same-species distinction.

rubric.why: A community consists of populations of different species living together.
rubric.description: Defines a community as populations of different species living in the same area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the different-species or multiple-population distinction.

modelAnswer: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area.
A community consists of populations of different species living together in the same area.

items.followUp: What hypothesis did A.F.A. King propose about mosquitoes and malaria?

rubric.why: King noted the association between mosquito abundance and malaria.
rubric.description: States that mosquitoes and malaria were observed together, particularly in places where mosquitoes were abundant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Protection from mosquito bites was associated with reduced malaria risk.
rubric.description: States that people protected from mosquito bites, such as by mosquito nets, were less likely to get malaria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

modelAnswer: A.F.A. King observed that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant.
He also observed that people protected from mosquito bites, for example by mosquito nets, were less likely to get malaria.

items.followUp: State two advantages of using quantitative data in biological investigations.

rubric.why: Numerical measurements make observations more precise and less subjective.
rubric.description: States that quantitative observations provide numerical, precise measurements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this advantage.

rubric.why: Numerical data can be compared and analysed systematically.
rubric.description: States that quantitative data can be compared, repeated or statistically analysed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one of these advantages.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations give numerical measurements, making results more precise and less subjective.
The measurements can be compared, repeated and analysed statistically.

items.followUp: Give two benefits of conserving biodiversity.

rubric.why: Biodiversity provides resources useful to people.
rubric.description: States one resource benefit of biodiversity, such as food, medicines or raw materials.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid resource benefit.

rubric.why: Biodiversity supports stable ecosystems and provides ecological or genetic benefits.
rubric.description: States one ecological or genetic benefit of biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid ecological or genetic benefit.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity provides useful resources such as food, medicines and raw materials.
It helps maintain ecological balance and stable ecosystems.
